questions.question: A fluid can be defined as a substance which _____ continuously when subjected to external _____ force.
questions.baby_explanation: A fluid is anything that can flow or spill, like water or air, whenever something pushes it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> A fluid deforms continuously under external shearing force. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: deforms, shearing
questions.common_mistake: Confusing 'shearing force' with 'normal force' (pressure).

questions.question: Which fluid type has the equation tau = mu(du/dy) + alpha E, with the example given as 'Liquid - solid Combinations in pipe flow'?

options.B: Visco-elastic fluid
options.C: Rheopectic fluid

questions.baby_explanation: This fluid acts a bit like a rubber band (elastic) and a bit like honey (viscous) at the same time.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Visco-elastic fluid combines viscous and elastic properties. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy) + alpha E -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Visco-elastic fluid
questions.common_mistake: Mixing it up with purely viscous time-dependent fluids like Thixotropic or Rheopectic.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of fluids according to the notes?

options.B: A small amount of shear stress causes continuous deformation
options.C: It does not conform to the shape of the containing vessel
options.D: It only deforms when a large normal force is applied

questions.baby_explanation: Even a tiny push makes a liquid change its shape completely, unlike a solid block of wood.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Characteristics of fluids: 1. No definite shape, conforms to vessel. 2. Small shear stress causes continuous deformation. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: A small amount of shear stress causes continuous deformation
questions.common_mistake: Assuming fluids need a large force to start deforming.

questions.question: What is the SI unit and formula for density (mass density) rho?

options.B: Mass / Volume, kg m^-3
options.C: Weight / Volume, N m^-3

questions.baby_explanation: Density is how much 'stuff' (mass) is packed into a specific amount of space (volume).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Density is the ratio of Mass of the fluid to its volume. -> Formula -> rho = Mass / Volume -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: Mass / Volume, kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Confusing mass density with specific weight (weight density).

questions.question: Specific volume is the reciprocal of _____ and it is commonly applied for _____.
questions.baby_explanation: Specific volume tells us how much space a certain weight of gas takes up. It's the exact opposite of density.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific volume = Volume / Mass, which is the reciprocal of mass density. -> Formula -> v = 1 / rho -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> m^3 kg^-1 -> Final answer: mass density, gases
questions.common_mistake: Stating it is applied for liquids instead of gases.

questions.question: What is the specific weight (w) formula and its standard value for water?

options.A: w = rho / g, value is 9.8 N m^-3
options.B: w = mass * volume, value is 1000 N m^-3
options.C: w = rho * g, value is 9.8 x 1000 N m^-3
options.D: w = weight / mass, value is 1000 kg m^-3

questions.baby_explanation: Specific weight measures how heavy a specific sized box of liquid feels because of gravity.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight (w) = Weight of fluid / Volume. -> Formula -> w = (Mass * g) / Volume = rho * g -> Substitution -> w = 1000 * 9.8 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: w = rho * g, value is 9.8 x 1000 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply the density of water (1000) by gravity (9.8).

questions.question: Specific gravity or relative gravity is defined as the ratio of density of the fluid to the density of standard fluid. For gases, the standard fluid is taken as:

options.B: steam
options.C: air

questions.baby_explanation: To see how heavy a gas is, we compare it to normal air, just like we compare liquids to water.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity = density of fluid / density of standard fluid. -> Formula -> SG_gas = rho_gas / rho_air -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> Unitless -> Final answer: air
questions.common_mistake: Assuming water is the standard reference for all fluids, including gases.

questions.question: Viscosity is defined as the property of fluid which offers _____ to the movement of one layer of the fluid over another adjacent layer.
questions.baby_explanation: Viscosity is fluid friction. It is what makes thick honey pour much slower than water.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Viscosity offers resistance to the movement of layers. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: resistance
questions.common_mistake: Using terms like 'assistance' or 'flow rate' instead of resistance.

questions.question: In the diagram showing velocity variation near a solid boundary, when two layers of a fluid at a distance dy move over each other, their velocities are shown as:

options.B: y and y + dy
options.C: u and u + du

questions.baby_explanation: Imagine two cars driving next to each other. One goes at speed u, and the other goes just a tiny bit faster at speed u plus a little extra (du).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The velocity profile diagram shows lower layer and upper layer. -> Formula -> Velocities are u (lower) and u + du (upper). -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: u and u + du
questions.common_mistake: Selecting y and y+dy, which represents the distance from the boundary, not the velocities.

questions.question: The top layer causes a _____ on the adjacent lower layer while the lower layer causes a shear stress on the adjacent top layer, which is directly proportional to the rate of _____.
questions.baby_explanation: Layers of fluid rub against each other. The rubbing force is called shear stress.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Interaction between fluid layers. -> Formula -> tau is proportional to du/dy (rate of shear strain). -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: shear stress, shear strain
questions.common_mistake: Confusing rate of shear strain with simple shear strain.

questions.question: In the equation tau = mu(du/dy), mu is the constant of proportionality. What is it called, and what is its SI unit?

options.B: Coefficient of dynamic viscosity, N s m^-2
options.C: Specific viscosity, kg m^-3

questions.baby_explanation: Mu is just a math symbol that tells us exactly how sticky and thick a fluid is in numbers.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> mu = tau / (du/dy). -> Formula -> Viscosity or coefficient of dynamic viscosity. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N s m^-2 (Newton seconds per meter square) -> Final answer: Coefficient of dynamic viscosity, N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Mixing up dynamic viscosity units (N s m^-2) with kinematic viscosity units (m^2 s^-1).

questions.question: Kinematic viscosity (nu) is defined as the ratio between _____ and the density of the fluid, and its SI unit is _____.
questions.baby_explanation: If dynamic viscosity is how thick the fluid is, kinematic viscosity is how thick it is compared to how heavy it is.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density. -> Formula -> nu = mu / rho -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> m^2 s^-1 -> Final answer: dynamic viscosity, m^2 s^-1
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting the ^-1 on the seconds in the SI unit.

questions.question: Newton's law of viscosity states that the shear stress on a fluid element layer is directly proportional to:

options.A: The distance dy from the boundary
options.B: The absolute velocity u
options.C: The pressure gradient
options.D: The velocity gradient or the rate of shear strain

questions.baby_explanation: Newton figured out that the harder you try to slide water layers past each other, the harder they resist you, in a perfectly straight line.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Newton's law of viscosity. -> Formula -> tau is directly proportional to du/dy. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: The velocity gradient or the rate of shear strain
questions.common_mistake: Thinking it is proportional to velocity itself, rather than the velocity gradient.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the classifications of fluids exactly as written in the notes?

options.A: A) liquid, gas and vapour. B) Real or viscous fluid, Ideal or inviscid fluid.
options.B: A) static, dynamic. B) compressible, incompressible.
options.C: A) Newtonian, non-Newtonian. B) Plastic, Thixotropic.

questions.baby_explanation: Fluids can be grouped into physical states (like water vs air) or how perfect they are (real vs imaginary).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Notes classify fluids under two main bullet points. -> Formula -> A) liquid, gas, vapour B) Real/viscous, Ideal/inviscid. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: A) liquid, gas and vapour. B) Real or viscous fluid, Ideal or inviscid fluid.
questions.common_mistake: Omitting 'vapour' from the physical state classification.

questions.question: According to the notes, a liquid is a fluid with definite volume which varies slightly with temperature and pressure, is assumed to be incompressible but undergoes viscosity.
questions.baby_explanation: A liquid like water takes up a specific amount of space. You can't squeeze it smaller easily, but it is still a bit sticky (viscous).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Liquid properties -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: True
questions.common_mistake: Assuming a liquid does not vary in volume at all with temperature.

questions.question: Gas completely fills the vessel which contains it. Vapour is a gas whose temperature and pressure are very near the _____ or _____ state.
questions.baby_explanation: Vapor is just a gas that is dangerously close to turning back into a liquid, like the fog above a boiling pot.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Vapour is a gas whose temperature and pressure are near the steam or liquid state. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: steam, liquid
questions.common_mistake: Confusing vapour with a completely stable gas like room-temperature oxygen.

questions.question: Which of the following describes Real or Viscous fluids based on the notes?

options.B: They are perfectly irrotational and incompressible.
options.C: They are actually available in nature, have viscosity (mu > 0), surface tension, density, and are compressible.
options.D: They do not follow Newton's law of viscosity under any circumstances.

questions.baby_explanation: Real fluids are the ones we actually see in the real world, like water and air. They all have some friction.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Real fluids exist in nature and have viscosity mu > 0, surface tension, and density. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: C
questions.common_mistake: Assuming real liquids are completely incompressible, whereas the notes state real fluids are compressible.

questions.question: For Newtonian fluids, the plot of the shear stress against the rate of deformation (du/dy) is a straight line through the origin. What does the slope of this line determine?

options.B: The specific weight of the fluid
options.C: The viscosity of the fluid
options.D: The yield stress of the fluid

questions.baby_explanation: If you draw a line on a graph for a regular fluid like water, how steep the line is tells you exactly how thick the water is.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> In a plot of tau vs du/dy, the slope determines viscosity. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy) -> Substitution -> slope = tau / (du/dy) = mu -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: The viscosity of the fluid
questions.common_mistake: Thinking the slope represents kinematic viscosity rather than absolute/dynamic viscosity.

questions.question: Ideal or Inviscid fluids do not exist in nature, have no viscosity (mu=0), no surface tension, and are irrotational and incompressible.
questions.baby_explanation: An ideal fluid is like a superhero fluid made up by scientists to make math easier. It has absolutely zero friction.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Ideal fluid -> Formula -> mu = 0, tau = 0 -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: True
questions.common_mistake: Believing ideal fluids can be found in a laboratory.

questions.question: Non-Newtonian fluids are generally complex mixtures and are studied under _____, which is a science of deformation and flow.
questions.baby_explanation: Rheology is just a fancy science word for studying how weird, gooey liquids squish and flow.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Science of deformation and flow -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: rheology
questions.common_mistake: Spelling it wrong or confusing it with topology.

questions.question: According to the notes on page 12, ideal plastics or Bingham plastic fluids have a definite yield stress. Which of the following is given as an example?

options.B: Blood
options.C: Sewage, sludge, drilling mud, water suspension of clay & flyash

questions.notes_flag: Inconsistency: Page 12 lists Bingham plastic formula as tau = Constant + mu(du/dy). Page 15 lists it as tau = tau_0 + mu(du/dy)^n with only water suspension of clay & flyash as an example.
questions.baby_explanation: Bingham plastics act like a solid plug until you push them hard enough, then they flow. Think of squeezing toothpaste!
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Bingham plastic has a yield stress before flowing. -> Formula -> tau = Constant + mu(du/dy) -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Sewage, sludge, drilling mud, water suspension of clay & flyash
questions.common_mistake: Mixing up Bingham plastics with Pseudoplastics like blood.

questions.question: A pseudoplastic fluid is a time-independent fluid with n < 1. Which of the following is listed as an example in the notes?

options.B: Crude oil
options.C: Printer ink
options.D: Paper pulp, rubber suspension paints, blood, milk, liquid cement and clay

questions.baby_explanation: These liquids get thinner and easier to stir the faster you mix them. Blood and milk act like this.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Pseudoplastic fluid -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n where n < 1. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Paper pulp, rubber suspension paints, blood, milk, liquid cement and clay
questions.common_mistake: Confusing n < 1 (Pseudoplastic) with n > 1 (Dilatant).

questions.question: A dilatant fluid is a time-independent fluid with n > 1. Which of the following is listed as an example?

options.A: Butter, printing inks, sugar solution, aqueous suspension
options.B: Blood and milk
options.C: Sewage and sludge

questions.notes_flag: Inconsistency: 'printing inks' is listed as Dilatant on page 13, but 'printer ink' is listed as Thixotropic on page 12/14.
questions.baby_explanation: These liquids get thicker and harder to stir the faster you mix them. It's like walking through deep mud.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Dilatant fluid -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n where n > 1. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Butter, printing inks, sugar solution, aqueous suspension
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting that dilatant is shear-thickening (n>1).

questions.question: A Thixotropic fluid has an equation tau = mu(du/dy)^n + f(t), where f(t) is _____. An example is printer ink or crude oil.
questions.baby_explanation: If you keep stirring this fluid, it gets thinner over time, even if you keep stirring at the same speed.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Thixotropic fluid is a time-dependent fluid. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n + f(t) -> Substitution -> f(t) is decreasing -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: decreasing
questions.common_mistake: Confusing it with Rheopectic fluids where f(t) is increasing.

questions.question: Which time-dependent fluid has an equation where f(t) is increasing, and gives 'Rare liquid Solid Suspension' as an example?

options.B: Thixotropic fluid
options.C: Rheopectic fluid

questions.baby_explanation: If you keep stirring this rare fluid, it gets thicker and thicker the longer you stir it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Rheopectic fluid is time-dependent. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n + f(t) -> Substitution -> f(t) is increasing -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Rheopectic fluid
questions.common_mistake: Mistaking it for a time-independent Dilatant fluid.

questions.question: In fluid mechanics, an ideal fluid is characterized primarily by which of the following theoretical traits?

options.A: It strictly obeys Newton's law of viscosity
options.B: It is completely frictionless and incompressible
options.C: It is highly viscous under high pressure
options.D: It possesses a high surface tension

questions.baby_explanation: An ideal fluid is like a magic perfect liquid. It never gets sticky or rubs against things (frictionless) and you can't squish it down into a smaller space (incompressible).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> An ideal fluid has no viscosity (mu=0) and is assumed irrotational and incompressible. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: It is completely frictionless and incompressible
questions.common_mistake: Confusing an 'ideal' fluid with a 'Newtonian' fluid (which does have viscosity).

questions.question: For a Newtonian fluid, the ratio of shear stress to the rate of shear strain (velocity gradient) remains perfectly constant regardless of how fast the fluid is deformed.
questions.baby_explanation: For normal liquids like water, the stickiness (viscosity) stays exactly the same no matter how fast you stir it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Newtonian fluids follow tau = mu(du/dy), meaning mu is a constant linear relationship. -> Formula -> mu = tau / (du/dy) = constant. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: True
questions.common_mistake: Thinking that stirring a Newtonian fluid faster increases its viscosity.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a fluid whose apparent viscosity decreases over time when subjected to a constant strain rate (shear-thinning over time)?

options.B: Dilatant fluid
options.C: Thixotropic fluid

questions.baby_explanation: If you stir it for a long time, it gets runnier and runnier, even if you don't stir it any faster. This is called thixotropic.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> A time-dependent fluid where resistance to flow decreases with time is a thixotropic fluid. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n + f(t) where f(t) is decreasing. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Thixotropic fluid
questions.common_mistake: Choosing Pseudoplastic, which is shear-thinning based on rate (time-independent), not based on time.

questions.question: On a standard rheological graph plotting shear stress on the y-axis against the rate of deformation (du/dy) on the x-axis, an Ideal Bingham plastic is represented by:

options.A: A curve that starts at the origin with a decreasing slope
options.B: A straight line starting from the origin
options.C: A straight line starting at a positive value on the y-axis

questions.baby_explanation: Imagine a graph where the line doesn't start at the bottom corner (zero). It starts higher up because you have to push the fluid hard before it starts moving at all, like pushing toothpaste out of a tube.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Bingham plastic has a distinct yield stress before it begins to flow linearly. -> Formula -> tau = Constant + mu(du/dy). -> Substitution -> At du/dy = 0, tau = Constant (yield stress > 0). -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: A straight line starting at a positive value on the y-axis
questions.common_mistake: Confusing it with a Newtonian fluid, which is a straight line starting exactly at the origin.

questions.question: In the general power-law equation for purely viscous non-Newtonian fluids, tau = mu(du/dy)^n, a dilatant fluid has an index n > 1, while a _____ fluid is modeled with n < 1.
questions.baby_explanation: Fluids that get thinner when you push them hard have a secret math number 'n' that is less than 1. Scientists call them pseudoplastic.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Time-independent fluids where n < 1 are categorized as pseudoplastics. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n (where n<1) -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: pseudoplastic
questions.common_mistake: Answering 'Thixotropic', missing the fact that thixotropic is time-dependent, while this equation describes time-independent fluids.

questions.question: When a fluid is perfectly at rest (static equilibrium), which of the following statements is true regarding the shear stress acting on it?

options.A: It is at its maximum value
options.B: It depends solely on the fluid's density
options.C: There is no shear stress or force acting on it
options.D: It is equal to the hydrostatic pressure

questions.baby_explanation: Fluids only get rubbing friction (shear stress) when they are moving and sliding. If water is just sitting completely still in a glass, there is zero rubbing friction.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Notes explicitly state: 'if the fluid is at rest, there is no shear stress or force acting on it'. -> Formula -> du/dy = 0, therefore tau = 0. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: There is no shear stress or force acting on it
questions.common_mistake: Assuming pressure and shear stress are the same thing (pressure acts normal to the surface even at rest, but shear stress is zero).

questions.question: While mass density is predominantly used to describe liquids, specific volume is more commonly applied to which phase of matter in fluid mechanics?

options.B: Gases
options.C: Visco-elastic fluids

questions.baby_explanation: Specific volume is mostly used by scientists when they are talking about gases like air or steam, because a small weight of gas can take up a huge amount of space.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific volume is the reciprocal of mass density and it is commonly applied for gases. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Gases
questions.common_mistake: Believing specific volume is a term exclusive to liquids because it has the word 'volume' in it.

questions.question: Specific gravity (or relative gravity) has the SI unit of kg m^-3 because it fundamentally measures the density of a fluid.
questions.baby_explanation: Specific gravity is just a ratio comparing two things (like comparing oil to water). Because it's just a comparison multiplier, it doesn't have any measurement units at all.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity is the ratio of two densities (rho_fluid / rho_standard). -> Formula -> (kg m^-3) / (kg m^-3) -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> Unitless -> Final answer: False
questions.common_mistake: Assuming specific gravity is just another phrase for density and assigning it density units.

questions.question: How is a liquid theoretically modeled in basic fluid mechanics regarding its volume response to external pressure?

options.B: It expands to fill its container completely
options.C: It is assumed to be incompressible

questions.baby_explanation: In simple math, we pretend that no matter how hard you squeeze a liquid like water, you can't make it take up less space.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Liquid has a definite volume which varies slightly with temp/pressure, but for calculations, it is assumed to be incompressible. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: It is assumed to be incompressible
questions.common_mistake: Confusing the behavior of gases (which expand to fill containers) with liquids.

questions.question: What distinguishes a vapour from a standard gas according to the fluid classification principles in the notes?

options.A: A vapour has a definite volume unlike a gas
options.B: A vapour cannot be compressed
options.C: A vapour's temperature and pressure are very near the steam or liquid state
options.D: A vapour follows Newton's law of viscosity perfectly, while a gas does not

questions.baby_explanation: A vapour is exactly like a gas, but it is super close to turning back into a liquid (like steam cooling down into water).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Vapour is a gas whose temperature and pressure are very near the steam or liquid state. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: A vapour's temperature and pressure are very near the steam or liquid state
questions.common_mistake: Thinking vapour and gas are completely unrelated states of matter with different volume properties.

questions.question: If 5.6 m^3 of an industrial oil weighs 46,800 N, what is its mass density (rho)? Assume the acceleration due to gravity g = 9.8 m s^-2.
questions.baby_explanation: First we find out how much the oil weighs per cubic meter. Then we divide by gravity to turn weight into mass. This tells us exactly how much 'stuff' is packed into one meter of space.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight (w) = Weight / Volume. Mass density (rho) = w / g. -> Formula -> w = Weight / Volume; rho = (Weight / Volume) / g -> Substitution -> w = 46800 / 5.6 = 8357.1428 N m^-3. rho = 8357.1428 / 9.8 = 852.769 -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: 852.77 kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Dividing the weight directly by the volume and calling that the mass density, forgetting to divide by gravity.

questions.question: A specific type of gas has a mass density of 1.25 kg m^-3. Calculate its specific volume.
questions.baby_explanation: Specific volume is just the upside-down version of density. If density is how heavy a box is, specific volume is how many boxes you need to fit a certain weight.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific volume is the reciprocal of mass density. -> Formula -> Specific volume = 1 / rho -> Substitution -> Specific volume = 1 / 1.25 = 0.8 -> Units -> m^3 kg^-1 -> Final answer: 0.8 m^3 kg^-1
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the density by gravity instead of taking the reciprocal.

questions.question: What is the specific weight (w) of a fluid that has a mass density of 850 kg m^-3? Assume g = 9.8 m s^-2.
questions.baby_explanation: We just multiply the mass (how much stuff there is) by gravity (how hard the earth pulls on it) to find its weight for every block of space.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight is mass density times gravity. -> Formula -> w = rho * g -> Substitution -> w = 850 * 9.8 = 8330 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: 8330 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Failing to multiply by gravity and assuming mass density and specific weight are identical.

questions.question: A fluid has an absolute dynamic viscosity (mu) of 0.048 N s m^-2. Assuming a linear velocity distribution from a solid wall, if the velocity is measured as 1.125 m/s at a distance of 75 mm from the wall, calculate the shear stress (tau) at the wall.
questions.baby_explanation: We find out how fast the speed changes compared to the distance, and then multiply that by how thick and sticky the fluid is.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Shear stress is viscosity times the velocity gradient. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du / dy) -> Substitution -> dy = 75 mm = 0.075 m. du/dy = 1.125 / 0.075 = 15 s^-1. tau = 0.048 * 15 = 0.72 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.72 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to convert 75 mm into meters (0.075 m).

questions.question: If the shear stress (tau) acting between two layers of a fluid is 2.5 N m^-2 and the dynamic viscosity (mu) of the fluid is 0.5 N s m^-2, what is the rate of shear strain (du/dy)?
questions.baby_explanation: If we know the pushing force (stress) and how thick the liquid is, we divide the force by the thickness to see how fast the liquid layers are sliding over each other.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Newton's law of viscosity relates shear stress and rate of shear strain. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du / dy) => du/dy = tau / mu -> Substitution -> du/dy = 2.5 / 0.5 = 5 -> Units -> s^-1 -> Final answer: 5 s^-1
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the stress and the viscosity together instead of dividing.

questions.question: Calculate the kinematic viscosity (nu) of a fluid whose dynamic viscosity (mu) is 0.003 N s m^-2 and mass density (rho) is 800 kg m^-3.
questions.baby_explanation: Kinematic viscosity is a way to see how thick a fluid is compared to how heavy it is. We just divide the thickness by the heaviness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to mass density. -> Formula -> nu = mu / rho -> Substitution -> nu = 0.003 / 800 = 0.00000375 -> Units -> m^2 s^-1 -> Final answer: 0.00000375 m^2 s^-1
questions.common_mistake: Dividing density by dynamic viscosity instead of the other way around.

questions.question: A container holds a fluid with a specific volume of 0.002 m^3 kg^-1. If the container's total volume is 10 m^3, what is the total mass of the fluid inside?
questions.baby_explanation: If 1 kilogram of this liquid takes up 0.002 blocks of space, we can figure out how many kilograms fit into 10 blocks of space by dividing 10 by 0.002.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific volume = Volume / Mass. -> Formula -> Mass = Volume / Specific volume -> Substitution -> Mass = 10 / 0.002 = 5000 -> Units -> kg -> Final answer: 5000 kg
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the volume and specific volume together, resulting in 0.02.

questions.question: The specific gravity of a fluid is 1.2. Calculate its specific weight (w), assuming the density of the standard fluid (water) is 1000 kg m^-3 and g = 9.8 m s^-2.
questions.baby_explanation: Specific gravity of 1.2 means the fluid is 1.2 times heavier than water. So we find the weight of water first, and then multiply it by 1.2.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity = rho_fluid / rho_water. Specific weight = rho_fluid * g. -> Formula -> rho_fluid = SG * rho_water; w = rho_fluid * g -> Substitution -> rho_fluid = 1.2 * 1000 = 1200. w = 1200 * 9.8 = 11760 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: 11760 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Calculating mass density (1200) and stopping there, without multiplying by gravity to find specific weight.

questions.question: For a dilatant fluid, the shear stress obeys the relationship tau = mu(du/dy)^n. If mu = 0.5, n = 1.2, and the velocity gradient du/dy is 10 s^-1, what is the shear stress?
questions.baby_explanation: This liquid gets thicker the faster you mix it. We take the mixing speed, raise it to a special power of 1.2, and then multiply by the stickiness constant.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Dilatant fluid shear stress formula. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy)^n -> Substitution -> tau = 0.5 * (10)^1.2 = 0.5 * 15.8489 = 7.9244 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 7.92 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Calculating 0.5 * 10 first, and then raising 5 to the power of 1.2, violating the order of operations.

questions.question: An ideal plastic (Bingham plastic) has a constant yield stress of 20 N m^-2. It flows with a constant linear relationship where the dynamic viscosity coefficient mu is 0.4 N s m^-2. If the rate of angular deformation (du/dy) is 15 s^-1, calculate the total shear stress (tau).
questions.baby_explanation: To move this toothpaste-like fluid, you first need 20 units of push just to break it loose. Then you add extra push based on how fast you want it to flow.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Bingham plastic linear relationship. -> Formula -> tau = Constant + mu(du/dy) -> Substitution -> tau = 20 + 0.4 * 15 = 20 + 6 = 26 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 26 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Ignoring the yield stress constant and only calculating 0.4 * 15 = 6.

questions.question: A cylindrical vessel of volume 2.5 m^3 is completely filled with an unknown fluid. The weight of the fluid inside is measured to be 19,600 N. Determine the specific gravity of this fluid. (Use standard water density = 1000 kg m^-3, g = 9.8 m s^-2).
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find out how heavy one square block of this liquid is. Then we compare it to a block of water. It turns out to be slightly lighter than water!
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity is the ratio of fluid density to standard water density. -> Formula -> w = Weight / Volume; rho_fluid = w / g; SG = rho_fluid / rho_water -> Substitution -> w = 19600 / 2.5 = 7840 N m^-3. rho_fluid = 7840 / 9.8 = 800 kg m^-3. SG = 800 / 1000 = 0.8 -> Units -> Unitless -> Final answer: 0.8
questions.common_mistake: Calculating specific weight (7840) and dividing it directly by the density of water (1000) without dividing by gravity first.

questions.question: An oil has a specific gravity of 0.85 and a kinematic viscosity (nu) of 1.5 x 10^-4 m^2 s^-1. Calculate its dynamic viscosity (mu). (Assume water density = 1000 kg m^-3).
questions.baby_explanation: We first use the specific gravity to find out how heavy the oil is. Then, knowing how it flows compared to its heaviness, we multiply them together to find its actual sticky friction.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by mass density. -> Formula -> rho_oil = SG * rho_water; mu = nu * rho_oil -> Substitution -> rho_oil = 0.85 * 1000 = 850 kg m^-3. mu = (1.5 * 10^-4) * 850 = 0.1275 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.1275 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Dividing the kinematic viscosity by the specific gravity instead of multiplying by the mass density.

questions.question: The velocity distribution over a solid boundary is given by the equation u = 2y - y^2 (where u is velocity in m/s and y is the perpendicular distance from the boundary in meters). If the dynamic viscosity of the fluid is 0.8 N s m^-2, what is the shear stress exactly at the solid boundary (y = 0)?
questions.baby_explanation: We have a math formula that tells us the speed at any distance. We use a math trick called a derivative to find the exact rate of change right at the wall, and multiply it by the stickiness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Newton's law of viscosity with a non-linear velocity profile. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy) -> Substitution -> u = 2y - y^2. Taking the derivative: du/dy = 2 - 2y. At the boundary (y=0), du/dy = 2 - 2(0) = 2 s^-1. tau = 0.8 * 2 = 1.6 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 1.6 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Failing to differentiate the velocity equation and just plugging in y=0 into the u equation, resulting in a zero velocity gradient.

questions.question: Gas A has a specific volume of 0.5 m^3 kg^-1. Gas B has a specific volume of 0.8 m^3 kg^-1. If 2 kg of Gas A and 3 kg of Gas B are mixed perfectly in a single container (without any chemical reaction or compression), what is the average mass density of the resulting mixture?
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find the total space Gas A takes up, and the total space Gas B takes up. We add those together to get the total volume. Then we divide the total weight by the total volume to find the new average density.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Mass density is Total Mass / Total Volume. -> Formula -> Volume_A = Mass_A * specific_volume_A; Volume_B = Mass_B * specific_volume_B. rho_mix = (Mass_A + Mass_B) / (Volume_A + Volume_B) -> Substitution -> Vol_A = 2 * 0.5 = 1.0 m^3. Vol_B = 3 * 0.8 = 2.4 m^3. Total Volume = 1.0 + 2.4 = 3.4 m^3. Total Mass = 2 + 3 = 5 kg. rho_mix = 5 / 3.4 = 1.4705 -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: 1.47 kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Averaging the two specific volumes (0.65) and taking the reciprocal, which ignores the different mass proportions.

questions.question: Two horizontal plates are placed 10 mm apart. The space between them is filled with a Newtonian fluid of dynamic viscosity 1.2 N s m^-2. The bottom plate is stationary, and the top plate is pulled with a force to maintain a constant velocity of 1.5 m/s. If the surface area of the top plate in contact with the fluid is 0.5 m^2, what is the total shear force required to maintain this motion? (Assume a linear velocity profile).
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find the rubbing friction (shear stress) created by sliding the top plate over the liquid. Since stress is just force divided by area, we multiply our stress by the total size of the plate to find the total pulling force needed.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Shear force is Shear Stress multiplied by the contact Area. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy); Force = tau * Area -> Substitution -> dy = 10 mm = 0.01 m. du/dy = 1.5 / 0.01 = 150 s^-1. tau = 1.2 * 150 = 180 N m^-2. Force = 180 * 0.5 = 90 -> Units -> N -> Final answer: 90 N
questions.common_mistake: Stopping at the calculation of shear stress (180 N m^-2) and forgetting to multiply by the plate area to find total force.

questions.question: If a certain brand of oil has a specific gravity of 0.85, what does this mathematically imply about its density compared to the standard fluid (water)?

options.B: Its density is 85% of the density of water
options.C: Its density is 1.85 times the density of water
options.D: It weighs 0.85 Newtons per cubic meter

questions.baby_explanation: Specific gravity is just a percentage score compared to water. A score of 0.85 means it is 85 percent as heavy as water.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity is the ratio of fluid density to standard fluid density. -> Formula -> SG = rho_fluid / rho_water -> Substitution -> 0.85 = rho_fluid / rho_water => rho_fluid = 0.85 * rho_water -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Its density is 85% of the density of water
questions.common_mistake: Assuming specific gravity represents the actual density value in standard units.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the physical significance of kinematic viscosity (nu)?

options.A: It represents the fluid's absolute resistance to shear stress irrespective of its mass.
options.B: It is the ratio of the fluid's inertia to its internal friction.
options.C: It represents the fluid's resistance to flow under its own weight, being the ratio of dynamic viscosity to mass density.
options.D: It measures the pressure variations inside a moving ideal fluid.

questions.baby_explanation: Kinematic viscosity looks at how thick a liquid is (dynamic viscosity) and divides it by how heavy it is (mass density) to see how well it pours under gravity.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity (nu) is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to density. -> Formula -> nu = mu / rho -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: It represents the fluid's resistance to flow under its own weight, being the ratio of dynamic viscosity to mass density.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing it with dynamic viscosity, which doesn't factor in the fluid's density.

questions.question: When stirring a pseudoplastic fluid vigorously, what observable change occurs in its flow behavior?

options.A: Its apparent viscosity increases, making it harder to stir.
options.B: Its apparent viscosity decreases, making it easier to stir.
options.C: It instantly turns into a solid plug.

questions.baby_explanation: Pseudoplastic liquids (like ketchup or milk) get thinner and easier to push the faster you move them around.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> A pseudoplastic fluid has n < 1, meaning its resistance (apparent viscosity) decreases as the rate of shear strain (stirring) increases. -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy)^n (n<1) -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Its apparent viscosity decreases, making it easier to stir.
questions.common_mistake: Confusing this with a dilatant fluid, which gets harder to stir.

questions.question: An ideal fluid is perfectly compressible, allowing its volume to adapt precisely to varying high-pressure conditions.
questions.baby_explanation: A superhero 'ideal' fluid cannot be squished at all. It is perfectly incompressible.

questions.question: A flat plate of area 1.5 m^2 is pulled over a stationary lower boundary with a constant velocity of 2 m/s. The gap between the boundaries is 0.05 m and is filled with a Newtonian fluid having a dynamic viscosity of 0.5 N s m^-2. Calculate the required pulling force.
questions.baby_explanation: We figure out how much rubbing friction there is per tiny square by dividing speed by gap size and multiplying by stickiness. Then we multiply that friction by the total number of squares (area) on the board.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Force = Shear Stress * Area. Shear stress = mu * (du/dy). -> Formula -> F = tau * A = (mu * (u/y)) * A -> Substitution -> tau = 0.5 * (2 / 0.05) = 20 N m^-2. F = 20 * 1.5 = 30 -> Units -> N -> Final answer: 30 N
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply the shear stress (20 N m^-2) by the plate's area.

questions.question: A liquid has a specific gravity of 0.9. Determine its specific weight (w) in N m^-3. (Assume density of standard fluid = 1000 kg m^-3, g = 9.8 m s^-2).
questions.baby_explanation: First we find out that the liquid is 0.9 times as heavy as water. Then we multiply that mass by gravity to find its actual pulling weight downward.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight is mass density times gravity. -> Formula -> rho_fluid = SG * rho_water; w = rho_fluid * g -> Substitution -> rho_fluid = 0.9 * 1000 = 900 kg m^-3. w = 900 * 9.8 = 8820 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: 8820 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the specific gravity directly by gravity (0.9 * 9.8 = 8.82) and skipping the density conversion.

questions.question: Water has a dynamic viscosity of 0.001 N s m^-2 and a mass density of 1000 kg m^-3. Calculate the kinematic viscosity (nu) of water.
questions.baby_explanation: We just take how thick water is and divide it by how heavy water is. The resulting tiny number is the kinematic viscosity.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity over density. -> Formula -> nu = mu / rho -> Substitution -> nu = 0.001 / 1000 = 0.000001 -> Units -> m^2 s^-1 -> Final answer: 0.000001 m^2 s^-1
questions.common_mistake: Writing the answer as 10^6 instead of 10^-6.

questions.question: The velocity u of a fluid near a solid boundary is given by u = 3y - y^2 (where y is distance from the boundary). If the dynamic viscosity mu is 0.2 N s m^-2, calculate the shear stress (tau) at a distance y = 1 m from the boundary.
questions.baby_explanation: We use a math rule to find exactly how fast the fluid speed is changing at a specific spot (1 meter away). Then we multiply that speed change by the fluid's stickiness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Shear stress at any point relies on the local velocity gradient du/dy. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy) -> Substitution -> u = 3y - y^2; du/dy = 3 - 2y. At y=1, du/dy = 3 - 2(1) = 1 s^-1. tau = 0.2 * 1 = 0.2 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.2 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Calculating the stress at the boundary (y=0) instead of the requested distance (y=1).

questions.question: On a graph plotting shear stress (tau) against the rate of deformation (du/dy), how is a non-Newtonian dilatant fluid visually represented compared to a Newtonian fluid?

questions.question: A gaseous substance has a specific volume of 0.4 m^3 kg^-1. Calculate its mass density (rho).
questions.baby_explanation: If one kilogram takes up 0.4 blocks of space, we can figure out how many kilograms fit in exactly one block by doing 1 divided by 0.4.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Mass density is the reciprocal of specific volume. -> Formula -> rho = 1 / v -> Substitution -> rho = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5 -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: 2.5 kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Squaring the value or multiplying by gravity instead of taking the simple reciprocal.

questions.question: A drilling mud behaves as an ideal Bingham plastic. It has a yield stress of 15 N m^-2 and a dynamic viscosity constant (mu) of 0.3 N s m^-2. Calculate the total shear stress required to induce a rate of shear strain (du/dy) of 10 s^-1.
questions.notes_flag: Inconsistency: Solved using the linear Bingham formula tau = Constant + mu(du/dy) from page 12, as n is not provided to use the non-linear formula from page 15.
questions.baby_explanation: First, you must push with 15 units of force just to break the mud loose so it isn't solid. Then you add extra pushing force based on how fast you want the mud layers to slide past each other.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Bingham plastic shear stress requires overcoming yield stress first. -> Formula -> tau = Yield_Stress + mu(du/dy) -> Substitution -> tau = 15 + 0.3 * 10 = 15 + 3 = 18 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 18 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the yield stress by the rate of strain, rather than adding them.

questions.question: A flat block of weight 100 N and contact area 0.2 m^2 slides down an inclined plane angled at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The plane is lubricated by a uniform 0.001 m thick oil film. If the block slides at a constant velocity of 1.5 m/s, calculate the dynamic viscosity (mu) of the oil. (Assume linear velocity profile).
questions.baby_explanation: First we find how hard gravity is pulling the block exactly parallel down the ramp. Then we divide that force by the block's area to find the rubbing stress. Finally, knowing how fast it slides and how thin the oil is, we calculate the oil's stickiness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Force causing motion equals shear force in the oil film at constant velocity. -> Formula -> F_parallel = Weight * sin(theta); tau = F_parallel / Area; mu = tau / (V / y) -> Substitution -> F_parallel = 100 * sin(30) = 50 N. tau = 50 / 0.2 = 250 N m^-2. du/dy = 1.5 / 0.001 = 1500 s^-1. mu = 250 / 1500 = 0.16667 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.1667 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Using the full weight (100 N) instead of the component of weight parallel to the incline (50 N).

questions.question: A tank contains 5 m^3 of a fluid. The fluid has a specific gravity of 1.2. Assuming the density of water is 1000 kg m^-3, what is the total mass of the fluid in the tank?
questions.baby_explanation: First, we use the specific gravity to find that the fluid is 1.2 times heavier than water per block. Then we multiply that weight by the 5 blocks of space it takes up.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity allows us to find density, and density * volume = mass. -> Formula -> rho_fluid = SG * rho_water; Mass = rho_fluid * Volume -> Substitution -> rho_fluid = 1.2 * 1000 = 1200 kg m^-3. Mass = 1200 * 5 = 6000 -> Units -> kg -> Final answer: 6000 kg
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying 1.2 by 5 directly (resulting in 6) without using the water density multiplier.

questions.question: A force of 50 N is required to maintain a constant velocity V on a flat plate of 2 m^2 area, moving over a solid surface. The gap is 0.02 m and is filled with a fluid of dynamic viscosity mu = 0.1 N s m^-2. Calculate the velocity V.
questions.baby_explanation: We know the total pushing force and the plate size, so we find the rubbing stress. We also know how thick the liquid is and how big the gap is, so we can work backward to figure out how fast the plate must be sliding.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Newton's law of viscosity. -> Formula -> tau = Force / Area; tau = mu * (V / y) -> Substitution -> tau = 50 / 2 = 25 N m^-2. 25 = 0.1 * (V / 0.02). 25 = 5 * V. V = 25 / 5 = 5 -> Units -> m/s -> Final answer: 5 m/s
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the gap by the force instead of dividing.

questions.question: A specific industrial fluid exhibits properties of both flowing honey and a bouncing rubber ball. According to the notes, which classification and equation applies?

options.B: Visco-elastic fluid: tau = mu(du/dy) + alpha E
options.C: Rheopectic fluid: tau = mu(du/dy)^n + f(t)

questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Visco-elastic fluid combines viscous flow and elastic strain (E). -> Formula -> tau = mu(du/dy) + alpha E -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Visco-elastic fluid: tau = mu(du/dy) + alpha E
questions.common_mistake: Confusing elastic behavior (spring back) with plastic behavior (yielding).

questions.question: A polymer solution behaves as a pseudoplastic non-Newtonian fluid governed by tau = mu(du/dy)^n. If the consistency index mu is 0.5, the flow behavior index n is 0.8, and the applied shear strain rate (du/dy) is 5 s^-1, calculate the exact shear stress developed.

questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Power-law calculation for pseudoplastic fluid. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy)^n -> Substitution -> tau = 0.5 * (5)^0.8 = 0.5 * 3.62389 = 1.8119 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 1.81 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Ignoring the exponent n and treating it as a Newtonian fluid (0.5 * 5 = 2.5).

questions.question: A fluid has a kinematic viscosity of 2 x 10^-5 m^2 s^-1 and a mass density of 950 kg m^-3. A square plate of 0.5 m by 0.5 m slides over a fixed boundary separated by a 0.002 m gap filled with this fluid. If the plate moves at 3 m/s, calculate the pulling force required.
questions.baby_explanation: This is a three-step puzzle. First, we use kinematic viscosity and density to find the fluid's actual stickiness. Then we find the rubbing stress by checking how fast the plate slides over the tiny gap. Finally, we multiply the stress by the plate's area.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> mu = nu * rho; tau = mu * (V / y); F = tau * Area. -> Formula -> mu = nu * rho; F = (nu * rho) * (V / y) * (L * W) -> Substitution -> mu = (2 * 10^-5) * 950 = 0.019 N s m^-2. tau = 0.019 * (3 / 0.002) = 28.5 N m^-2. Area = 0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25 m^2. F = 28.5 * 0.25 = 7.125 -> Units -> N -> Final answer: 7.125 N
questions.common_mistake: Using the kinematic viscosity directly in the shear stress formula instead of converting it to dynamic viscosity first.

questions.question: The velocity profile of a Newtonian fluid flowing near a boundary is u = 1.5 * y^(0.5) (where u is m/s and y is meters). The dynamic viscosity of the fluid is 0.04 N s m^-2. Calculate the shear stress exactly at a distance y = 0.04 m from the boundary.
questions.baby_explanation: The speed of the fluid changes depending on a square root curve. We use calculus to find the exact slope of that curve at 0.04 meters away, and multiply it by the fluid's stickiness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Non-linear velocity gradient requiring differentiation. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy) -> Substitution -> u = 1.5 * y^(0.5); du/dy = 1.5 * 0.5 * y^(-0.5) = 0.75 / sqrt(y). At y = 0.04, du/dy = 0.75 / sqrt(0.04) = 0.75 / 0.2 = 3.75 s^-1. tau = 0.04 * 3.75 = 0.15 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.15 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to differentiate and just plugging y=0.04 directly into the u equation.

questions.question: A highly compressed gaseous fluid has a specific gravity of 0.8 compared to standard water (density 1000 kg m^-3). What is the specific volume of this fluid?
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find how dense the gas is by comparing it to water. Then, since specific volume is just the upside-down version of density, we divide 1 by our density number.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific volume is the reciprocal of mass density. -> Formula -> rho_fluid = SG * rho_water; v = 1 / rho_fluid -> Substitution -> rho_fluid = 0.8 * 1000 = 800 kg m^-3. v = 1 / 800 = 0.00125 -> Units -> m^3 kg^-1 -> Final answer: 0.00125 m^3 kg^-1
questions.common_mistake: Finding the density (800) and failing to take the reciprocal to find specific volume.

questions.question: Newton's law of viscosity establishes a linear relationship between which two fundamental fluid mechanics variables?

questions.question: When calculating the specific gravity of a gas, the density of the gas is divided by the density of the standard fluid, which is taken as _____.

questions.question: A certain fluid is observed to become significantly less viscous the longer it is subjected to a constant shearing force. Which category does this fluid belong to?

questions.question: In an ideal flow, why is there absolutely no existence of shear force regardless of the fluid's motion?

options.A: Because the fluid velocity is always zero
options.B: Because of vanishing viscosity (mu = 0)
options.C: Because the fluid is compressible

questions.question: A fluid layer is bounded by two large parallel plates placed 15 mm apart. The upper plate moves at 2.5 m/s, and the lower plate is stationary. If the shear stress on the upper plate is 30 N m^-2, calculate the dynamic viscosity (mu) of the fluid.
questions.baby_explanation: We know the rubbing friction, the speed, and the gap size. We use a math formula to divide the friction by the speed change over that gap to find out how sticky the fluid is.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Dynamic viscosity is shear stress divided by the velocity gradient. -> Formula -> mu = tau / (du/dy) -> Substitution -> dy = 0.015 m, du = 2.5 m/s. du/dy = 2.5 / 0.015 = 166.67 s^-1. mu = 30 / 166.67 = 0.18 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.18 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to convert the gap distance from millimeters (15) to meters (0.015).

questions.question: The specific volume of an ideal gas is measured as 1.25 m^3 kg^-1. Calculate the specific weight (w) of this gas. (Assume g = 9.8 m s^-2).
questions.baby_explanation: First, we turn specific volume upside-down to find the density. Then, we multiply that density by the pull of gravity to find how heavy one block of this gas really is.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Density is reciprocal of specific volume; specific weight is density times gravity. -> Formula -> rho = 1 / v; w = rho * g -> Substitution -> rho = 1 / 1.25 = 0.8 kg m^-3. w = 0.8 * 9.8 = 7.84 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: 7.84 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying specific volume directly by gravity (1.25 * 9.8) instead of finding density first.

questions.question: A liquid has a dynamic viscosity of 0.08 N s m^-2 and a specific gravity of 0.9. What is its kinematic viscosity (nu)? (Assume water density = 1000 kg m^-3).
questions.baby_explanation: First we find the liquid's actual weight by multiplying its specific gravity score by water's weight. Then we divide its stickiness by that actual weight.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity = Dynamic viscosity / Mass density. -> Formula -> rho_fluid = SG * rho_water; nu = mu / rho_fluid -> Substitution -> rho_fluid = 0.9 * 1000 = 900 kg m^-3. nu = 0.08 / 900 = 0.00008888... -> Units -> m^2 s^-1 -> Final answer: 0.00008889 m^2 s^-1
questions.common_mistake: Dividing the dynamic viscosity directly by the specific gravity (0.08 / 0.9) instead of the absolute density.

questions.question: A dilatant fluid (like a sugar solution) has a flow behavior index n = 1.5 and a consistency index mu = 0.2. If the rate of shear strain (du/dy) is 4 s^-1, what is the resulting shear stress?
questions.baby_explanation: Because it's dilatant, it gets super thick when pushed. We take the pushing speed, raise it to the power of 1.5 on our calculator, and multiply it by the fluid's stickiness number.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Dilatant fluid follows the power law tau = mu(du/dy)^n with n > 1. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy)^n -> Substitution -> tau = 0.2 * (4)^1.5. Since 4^1.5 = sqrt(4^3) = sqrt(64) = 8. tau = 0.2 * 8 = 1.6 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 1.6 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Calculating 0.2 * 4 first to get 0.8, and then raising 0.8 to the power of 1.5.

questions.question: The specific weight of water on Earth is given as 9.8 x 1000 N m^-3. If 2.5 m^3 of this water is moved to a hypothetical planet where the acceleration due to gravity is 5.0 m s^-2, what is the new specific weight of the water?
questions.baby_explanation: Weight changes depending on what planet you are on. The amount of stuff (mass density) in water stays the same (1000), but we multiply it by the new, weaker gravity (5.0).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight (w) relies on local gravity (w = rho * g), while mass density (rho) is independent of gravity. -> Formula -> rho = 1000 kg m^-3 (constant); w_new = rho * g_new -> Substitution -> w_new = 1000 * 5.0 = 5000 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: 5000 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Assuming specific weight is a constant property of the fluid like density, and answering 9800.

questions.question: A perfectly mixed solution consists of 1000 kg of water (density = 1000 kg m^-3) and 800 kg of an oil (density = 800 kg m^-3). Assuming the volumes are perfectly additive, calculate the mass density of the final mixture.
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find out exactly how much space the water takes up and how much space the oil takes up. Add those spaces together. Then, divide the total combined weight by the total combined space.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Mixture density = Total Mass / Total Volume. -> Formula -> Vol_water = Mass_water / rho_water; Vol_oil = Mass_oil / rho_oil; rho_mix = (Mass_water + Mass_oil) / (Vol_water + Vol_oil) -> Substitution -> Vol_water = 1000 / 1000 = 1 m^3. Vol_oil = 800 / 800 = 1 m^3. Total Volume = 2 m^3. Total Mass = 1800 kg. rho_mix = 1800 / 2 = 900 -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: 900 kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Just averaging the two densities because the masses are similar, without calculating the exact volumes.

questions.question: A cylindrical shaft of 0.1 m diameter rotates continuously at a steady speed inside a fixed sleeve. The clearance between the shaft and the sleeve is 0.002 m and is filled with oil having a kinematic viscosity of 1.2 x 10^-4 m^2 s^-1 and specific gravity 0.85. If the linear surface velocity of the shaft is 2 m/s, calculate the shear stress acting on the surface of the shaft. (Assume a linear velocity profile).
questions.baby_explanation: This is a big puzzle. First, we find the oil's actual stickiness by combining its kinematic viscosity and its heaviness (density). Then we find the rubbing friction by dividing the shaft's speed by the tiny gap between the shaft and the sleeve.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> tau = mu * (du/dy), where mu = nu * (SG * rho_water). -> Formula -> mu = nu * (SG * 1000); tau = mu * (V / gap) -> Substitution -> mu = (1.2 * 10^-4) * (0.85 * 1000) = (1.2 * 10^-4) * 850 = 0.102 N s m^-2. tau = 0.102 * (2 / 0.002) = 0.102 * 1000 = 102 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 102 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply by 1000 to convert specific gravity to mass density before calculating dynamic viscosity.

questions.question: A liquid is tested in a viscometer. When the rate of shear strain (du/dy) is 2 s^-1, the shear stress is measured as 4 N m^-2. When the rate of shear strain is increased to 4 s^-1, the shear stress becomes 6.5 N m^-2. Using the purely viscous power-law equation tau = mu(du/dy)^n, solve for the flow behavior index (n).
questions.baby_explanation: We have two clues about how this liquid acts at different speeds. By dividing the two clues mathematically, we can figure out the special power number 'n' that defines this fluid's behavior.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Use the power-law equation to set up a ratio. -> Formula -> tau_1 = mu*(du/dy)_1^n; tau_2 = mu*(du/dy)_2^n. Ratio: tau_2 / tau_1 = ((du/dy)_2 / (du/dy)_1)^n -> Substitution -> 6.5 / 4 = (4 / 2)^n. 1.625 = 2^n. Take log base 10 of both sides: log(1.625) = n * log(2). n = log(1.625) / log(2) = 0.21085 / 0.30103 = 0.700 -> Units -> Unitless -> Final answer: 0.7
questions.common_mistake: Assuming it is a Newtonian fluid and trying to find a constant mu, failing to realize the ratio is non-linear.

questions.question: The velocity distribution of a fluid flow over a flat surface is given by u = (3/4)y - y^2, where u is the velocity in m/s and y is the distance from the surface in meters. The fluid has a dynamic viscosity of 0.85 N s m^-2. Determine the shear stress at a distance of 0.2 m from the surface.
questions.baby_explanation: First, we use a calculus trick on the speed formula to find exactly how fast the fluid layers are scraping against each other 0.2 meters away from the wall. Then we multiply that scraping rate by the stickiness of the fluid.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Calculate local velocity gradient using derivative, then apply Newton's Law. -> Formula -> du/dy = d/dy ((3/4)y - y^2); tau = mu * (du/dy) -> Substitution -> du/dy = 0.75 - 2y. At y = 0.2: du/dy = 0.75 - 2(0.2) = 0.75 - 0.4 = 0.35 s^-1. tau = 0.85 * 0.35 = 0.2975 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.2975 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting to apply the derivative and just multiplying the viscosity by the velocity at y=0.2.

questions.question: An unknown gas has a specific gravity of 1.5 relative to standard air. If the density of standard air is 1.2 kg m^-3, what is the specific weight (w) of this gas? (Assume g = 9.8 m s^-2).
questions.baby_explanation: First we multiply the specific gravity by the weight of air to find the gas's density. Then we multiply by gravity to find its true weight downward.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity of gas = rho_gas / rho_air. Specific weight = rho * g. -> Formula -> rho_gas = SG * rho_air; w = rho_gas * g -> Substitution -> rho_gas = 1.5 * 1.2 = 1.8 kg m^-3. w = 1.8 * 9.8 = 17.64 -> Units -> N m^-3 -> Final answer: 17.64 N m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Using the density of water (1000) instead of the density of air (1.2) for a gas.

questions.question: A spherical object falls through a fluid. The fluid exerts a shear stress, and we know the fluid's kinematic viscosity is 4 x 10^-6 m^2 s^-1 and its specific weight is 8330 N m^-3. Calculate the fluid's dynamic viscosity (mu). (Assume g = 9.8 m s^-2).
questions.baby_explanation: First we divide the heavy pulling weight by gravity to find the actual mass density of the fluid. Once we have the mass, we multiply it by the kinematic viscosity to find the true stickiness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight = rho * g; mu = nu * rho. -> Formula -> rho = w / g; mu = nu * rho -> Substitution -> rho = 8330 / 9.8 = 850 kg m^-3. mu = (4 * 10^-6) * 850 = 0.0034 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.0034 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying the kinematic viscosity directly by the specific weight, missing the conversion to mass density via gravity.

questions.question: A space of 0.03 m between two large flat plates is filled with an oil of specific gravity 0.88 and dynamic viscosity 0.5 N s m^-2. A thin, flat square plate of 0.4 m by 0.4 m is pulled continuously through the oil at a velocity of 2 m/s. The thin plate is positioned exactly in the middle of the 0.03 m gap. Calculate the total force required to drag this thin plate.
questions.baby_explanation: The thin plate is in the middle of a gap, so it is dragging against oil on both its top side AND its bottom side. We have to calculate the rubbing friction for one side, multiply it by the plate's area, and then double it because of the two sides.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Force is required to overcome shear stress on BOTH sides of the thin plate. -> Formula -> gap_1 = gap_2 = total_gap / 2. tau = mu * (V / gap_1). F_one_side = tau * Area. F_total = 2 * F_one_side -> Substitution -> gap_1 = 0.03 / 2 = 0.015 m. tau = 0.5 * (2 / 0.015) = 66.6667 N m^-2. Area = 0.4 * 0.4 = 0.16 m^2. F_one_side = 66.6667 * 0.16 = 10.6667 N. F_total = 10.6667 * 2 = 21.333 -> Units -> N -> Final answer: 21.33 N
questions.common_mistake: Only calculating the force for one side of the plate, resulting in half the correct answer (10.67 N).

questions.question: A sludge behaves as a Bingham plastic. In a laboratory test, when the rate of shear strain is 5 s^-1, the measured shear stress is 25 N m^-2. When the rate of shear strain is increased to 10 s^-1, the shear stress becomes 40 N m^-2. Assuming the linear relation tau = Constant + mu(du/dy), calculate the yield stress (the Constant).
questions.baby_explanation: We use a little algebra to find the slope of the line (how sticky the fluid is). Once we know that, we can easily backtrack to find exactly where the line starts on the graph (the initial force needed to break the sludge loose).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Use two data points to solve a system of linear equations for a Bingham plastic. -> Formula -> tau = tau_yield + mu(du/dy). 25 = tau_yield + mu(5); 40 = tau_yield + mu(10). -> Substitution -> Subtract the first from the second: 15 = mu(5) => mu = 3 N s m^-2. Substitute mu back into the first equation: 25 = tau_yield + 3(5) => 25 = tau_yield + 15 => tau_yield = 10 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 10 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Calculating mu correctly (3) but presenting that as the final answer instead of the yield stress.

questions.question: An industrial storage tank holds 3.5 m^3 of a chemical fluid. The fluid has a specific gravity of 0.8. Calculate the total mass of the fluid in kilograms. (Assume water density = 1000 kg m^-3).
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find out that the chemical is 0.8 times as heavy as water, meaning it weighs 800 kg for every block of space. Then we multiply that by the 3.5 blocks of space it takes up.

questions.question: A fluid with a dynamic viscosity of 0.45 N s m^-2 is located between two parallel boundaries separated by a gap of 0.03 m. The lower boundary is fixed, and the upper boundary moves at 1.5 m/s. Calculate the shear stress.

questions.question: A flat plate of area 1.2 m^2 is pulled over a fluid film 0.004 m thick with a velocity of 0.5 m/s. The dynamic viscosity of the fluid is 0.8 N s m^-2. What is the total shear force required?
questions.baby_explanation: We find the rubbing friction per tiny square first by dividing speed by thickness and multiplying by stickiness. Then we multiply that friction by the total number of squares (area) on the plate.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Force = Shear Stress * Area. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (V / y); F = tau * Area -> Substitution -> tau = 0.8 * (0.5 / 0.004) = 0.8 * 125 = 100 N m^-2. F = 100 * 1.2 = 120 -> Units -> N -> Final answer: 120 N

questions.question: A time-independent non-Newtonian pseudoplastic fluid follows tau = mu(du/dy)^n. If mu = 0.5, n = 0.5, and the rate of shear strain (du/dy) is 9 s^-1, calculate the shear stress.

questions.question: An ideal Bingham plastic has a yield stress of 25 N m^-2. Its dynamic viscosity coefficient (mu) is 0.6 N s m^-2. If the rate of angular deformation (du/dy) is 5 s^-1, what is the total shear stress?

The gap between the plates is 0.002 m and is filled with an unknown fluid. A pulling force of 150 N is required to maintain this motion. Determine the dynamic viscosity (mu) of the fluid.
questions.baby_explanation: First, we find the area of the square plate. We divide the total pulling force by this area to find the rubbing stress. Then we work backward from the speed and the gap size to figure out how sticky the fluid must be.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> F = tau * A, tau = mu * (V / y). -> Formula -> A = L * W; tau = F / A; mu = tau / (V / y) -> Substitution -> A = 0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25 m^2. tau = 150 / 0.25 = 600 N m^-2. du/dy = 4 / 0.002 = 2000 s^-1. mu = 600 / 2000 = 0.3 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.3 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Using the dimensions 0.5 directly as the area, rather than calculating 0.5 * 0.5.

questions.question: You have 4 m^3 of Fluid A (specific gravity = 0.8) and 2 m^3 of Fluid B (specific gravity = 1.1). If you mix them together perfectly without any change in total volume, what is the mass density of the resulting mixture? (Assume water density = 1000 kg m^-3).
questions.baby_explanation: First we calculate the exact mass (weight) of Fluid A, then the exact mass of Fluid B. We add the two weights together, add the two volumes together, and divide the total weight by the total volume.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Mixture density = Total Mass / Total Volume. -> Formula -> rho_A = 0.8 * 1000; Mass_A = rho_A * Vol_A. rho_B = 1.1 * 1000; Mass_B = rho_B * Vol_B. rho_mix = (Mass_A + Mass_B) / (Vol_A + Vol_B) -> Substitution -> rho_A = 800, Mass_A = 800 * 4 = 3200 kg. rho_B = 1100, Mass_B = 1100 * 2 = 2200 kg. Total Mass = 3200 + 2200 = 5400 kg. Total Vol = 4 + 2 = 6 m^3. rho_mix = 5400 / 6 = 900 -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: 900 kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Averaging the two specific gravities directly ( (0.8+1.1)/2 = 0.95 ) and getting 950, completely ignoring the different volume amounts.

questions.question: An example of a visco-elastic fluid given in the notes is 'Liquid - solid Combinations in _____ flow'.

questions.question: Which of the following sets of properties completely defines a 'Real or Viscous fluid' as described in the notes?

options.B: Viscosity (mu > 0), surface tension, density, and compressible

questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Direct extraction from page 10. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Viscosity (mu > 0), surface tension, density, and compressible

questions.question: In the context of the shear stress proportionality formula, the 'rate of deformation' is synonymous with which other term heavily used in the notes?

options.B: Velocity potential
options.C: Rate of shear strain (du/dy)

questions.baby_explanation: The rate at which a fluid bends and deforms is exactly the same thing as how fast its layers are sliding past each other (rate of shear strain).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The notes repeatedly equate 'velocity gradient', 'rate of shear strain', and 'rate of deformation' as du/dy. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Rate of shear strain (du/dy)
questions.common_mistake: Confusing it with simple shear strain (lacking the 'rate of' aspect).

questions.question: According to the notes, specific volume is a metric that is commonly applied for liquids.

questions.question: A substance has a specific weight of 8820 N m^-3. Calculate its mass density (rho). (Assume g = 9.8 m s^-2).
questions.baby_explanation: To turn the heavy pulling weight back into the actual amount of stuff (mass), we just divide the weight by gravity.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific weight = Mass density * gravity. -> Formula -> rho = w / g -> Substitution -> rho = 8820 / 9.8 = 900 -> Units -> kg m^-3 -> Final answer: 900 kg m^-3
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying by 9.8 instead of dividing.

questions.question: A dilatant fluid follows tau = mu(du/dy)^n. Given a consistency index mu = 0.1, a flow behavior index n = 2, and a shear strain rate of 10 s^-1, calculate the shear stress.
questions.baby_explanation: This fluid gets much thicker when you push it. We square the pushing speed (10 times 10 is 100) and then multiply it by the fluid's stickiness number (0.1).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Power-law calculation. -> Formula -> tau = mu * (du/dy)^n -> Substitution -> tau = 0.1 * (10)^2 = 0.1 * 100 = 10 -> Units -> N m^-2 -> Final answer: 10 N m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Multiplying 0.1 by 10 first to get 1, and then squaring 1 to get 1.

questions.question: Calculate the dynamic viscosity (mu) of an oil if its kinematic viscosity (nu) is 1.2 x 10^-4 m^2 s^-1 and its specific gravity is 0.85. (Assume water density = 1000 kg m^-3).
questions.baby_explanation: First we figure out the oil's actual mass density by multiplying its score by water's weight. Then we multiply that mass by the kinematic viscosity to find its true stickiness.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Kinematic viscosity = Dynamic viscosity / density. -> Formula -> rho = SG * 1000; mu = nu * rho -> Substitution -> rho = 0.85 * 1000 = 850. mu = (1.2 * 10^-4) * 850 = 0.102 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 0.102 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Failing to multiply by 1000 to convert specific gravity into mass density.

questions.question: In the non-Newtonian purely viscous fluid equations mapped out in the notes, what mathematical feature explicitly dictates whether a time-dependent fluid is classified as Thixotropic or Rheopectic?

options.A: Whether the flow behavior index 'n' is greater than or less than 1
options.B: Whether the time function f(t) is decreasing or increasing
options.C: Whether the yield stress constant is zero or positive
options.D: Whether the fluid is mixed with a solid suspension

questions.baby_explanation: Thixotropic means it gets runnier over time (decreasing math function). Rheopectic means it gets thicker over time (increasing math function).
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> According to the table on page 14, both use tau = mu(du/dy)^n + f(t). For Thixotropic, f(t) is decreasing. For Rheopectic, f(t) is increasing. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: Whether the time function f(t) is decreasing or increasing
questions.common_mistake: Selecting option A, which applies to time-independent fluids (Pseudoplastic vs Dilatant).

questions.question: A block weighing 500 N and having a flat base area of 0.2 m^2 slides down a ramp inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The ramp is coated with a 0.001 m thick oil film. If the block descends at a steady velocity of 1 m/s, calculate the dynamic viscosity of the oil. (Assume a linear velocity profile).
questions.baby_explanation: Gravity pulls the block straight down, but only part of that pulling force actually drags it along the ramp. We divide that dragging force by the block's area to find the rubbing stress. Finally, we divide that stress by how fast the speed changes over the tiny gap.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Force parallel to incline = Weight * sin(theta). tau = F_parallel / Area. mu = tau / (V / y). -> Formula -> F_p = W * sin(30); tau = F_p / A; mu = tau / (V / y) -> Substitution -> F_p = 500 * 0.5 = 250 N. tau = 250 / 0.2 = 1250 N m^-2. du/dy = 1 / 0.001 = 1000 s^-1. mu = 1250 / 1000 = 1.25 -> Units -> N s m^-2 -> Final answer: 1.25 N s m^-2
questions.common_mistake: Using the full 500 N weight to calculate shear stress, rather than using sine to find the parallel component.

questions.question: What is the specific gravity of standard liquid water under typical conditions, according to the fluid mechanics convention?
questions.baby_explanation: Specific gravity is a comparison to water. If you compare water to itself, it is exactly the same, so the score is exactly 1.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Specific gravity = density of fluid / density of standard fluid. -> Formula -> SG_water = rho_water / rho_water -> Substitution -> SG_water = 1000 / 1000 = 1 -> Units -> Unitless -> Final answer: 1
questions.common_mistake: Answering 1000, which is the density in kg/m^3, not the unitless specific gravity.

questions.question: An ideal fluid must have a constant density throughout its flow, as it is strictly defined as incompressible.
questions.baby_explanation: A perfect, imaginary superhero fluid cannot be squeezed at all. Because it can't be squeezed, its density (how packed its stuff is) never changes.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Ideal fluids are defined in the notes as incompressible. -> Formula -> Incompressible means density (rho) = constant. -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> N/A -> Final answer: True
questions.common_mistake: Confusing ideal fluids with ideal gases, which are highly compressible.

questions.question: The SI unit of kinematic viscosity (nu) is stated in the notes as _____.
questions.baby_explanation: Kinematic viscosity uses a unit that combines square meters and seconds. It tells us how the fluid's stickiness spreads out over an area in a given time.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Verbatim from notes page 8. -> Formula -> N/A -> Substitution -> N/A -> Units -> m^2 s^-1 -> Final answer: m^2 s^-1

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of a real fluid according to the provided notes?

options.B: It is compressible
options.C: It is irrotational
